A Stackelberg Game Framework with Drainability Guardrails for Pricing and Scaling in Multi-Tenant GPU Cloud Platforms

Junji Yan    Asrin Efe Yorulmaz    Hanchen Zhou    Tamer Başar ††thanks: This work was supported in part by the IBM-ILLINOIS Discovery Accelerator Institute (IIDAI) under Grant #122955. Junji Yan, Asrin Efe Yorulmaz, and Tamer Başar are with the Coordinated Science Laboratory (CSL), University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC), Urbana, IL 61801, USA. Hanchen Zhou was also with CSL, UIUC; he is now with CFINS, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China. Emails: {junjiy2, ay20, basar1}@illinois.edu, zhouhc22@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn.
Abstract

Modern Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)-backed services must satisfy strict latency service-level objectives (SLOs) while controlling spare-capacity cost. In multi-tenant GPU cloud platforms, this trade-off is inherently dynamic because workload demand is endogenous; specifically, pricing shapes the submissions of heterogeneous tenants, which subsequently impact congestion and delay. We formulate the joint pricing-and-scaling problem as a large-population Stackelberg game problem, and we derive an explicit equilibrium demand map. The resulting closed-loop model reveals a structural failure mode in which delay-insensitive workloads sustain a residual demand floor, making the backlog undrainable under bounded price and service capacity. This observation motivates a computable drainability guardrail that certifies uniformly negative drift in the residual-demand regime. For any fixed price-capacity pair satisfying the drainability guardrail, we establish a unique operating point and global convergence towards it under a checkable step-size condition. Building on this fixed-pair analysis, we further develop an optimizer-agnostic action shield for the full dynamic problem and show empirically that it improves safety and robustness for model-free reinforcement learning (RL) in this setting.

I Introduction

In recent years, latency-oriented service-level objectives (SLOs) have become a hard constraint for many Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)-backed services. Meanwhile, meeting SLOs under bursty demand often requires keeping spare GPU capacity online, which can substantially increase costs [1]. GPU platforms therefore face a persistent tension: they must maintain service quality while limiting the cost of excess capacity in systems with frictional capacity adjustment. This challenge has motivated a growing body of work on SLO-aware GPU serving and capacity management [2, 3].

Most existing SLO-aware serving and autoscaling systems focus on the supply side and treat workload demand as externally given [4, 5]. In multi-tenant GPU cloud platforms, however, demand is often endogenous and shaped dynamically by posted prices and congestion. The posted price acts as a direct demand-side lever, influencing which tenants participate and how aggressively they submit work, while congestion-induced delay feeds back into demand as service quality changes. Consequently, SLO-aware operation requires managing both capacity and demand in a closed loop.

To address this gap, we study a joint price–capacity control problem for a multi-tenant GPU cloud platform in a closed loop, aiming to maximize long-run profit while meeting latency SLO constraints. We adopt a Stackelberg game formulation [6] to make the demand-side feedback explicit. At each decision epoch, the platform, leader, posts a unit price and a capacity target, and tenants, followers, respond by choosing submission rates based on the posted price and the public congestion signal. To capture heterogeneity, we approximate the population by finitely many mean-field types [7] with distinct price and delay sensitivities, including delay-insensitive but price-sensitive types that represent opportunistic or speculative demand. Each type solves a strictly concave stage-wise problem, yielding a unique best response. Aggregating across types gives a unique equilibrium demand map, which, together with the backlog recursion and frictional capacity dynamics, induces a low-dimensional closed-loop system.

This Stackelberg formulation also reveals a structural failure mode that is absent in exogenous-demand formulations and therefore prevents a direct move to nominal dynamic optimization. That is, under admissible leader actions, the system may become undrainable in the high-congestion regime. This issue arises for two main reasons. First, although demand can change rapidly, physical GPU capacity adjusts slowly due to provisioning frictions, such as cold starts [8], setup delays [9], and scale-down inertia [10]. Moreover, frequent capacity adjustments can induce oscillations and incur switching costs. Second, tenant demand responses to price and congestion are heterogeneous and need not vanish uniformly as congestion grows. Specifically, while delay-sensitive users eventually drop out, delay-insensitive types continue submitting work, sustaining a residual demand floor. As a result, even under severe congestion, the platform may continue to face persistent demand pressure. These observations motivate characterizing the admissible leader actions under which the backlog remains in a stable and drainable regime.

Such a structural characterization is a necessary prerequisite for dynamic learning. Standard model-free reinforcement learning (RL) relies on trial-and-error exploration [11] and may sample actions that push the system into an undrainable regime. Given capacity frictions and persistent residual demand under congestion, recovery can be difficult and service quality may degrade. Explicitly identifying the drainable action region thus provides a theoretical guardrail that naturally translates into an action shield [12], enabling safe exploration of joint pricing and scaling policies while preserving drainability and pursuing long-run profit subject to SLO compliance.

Related Work.  Our work relates to several lines of research on cloud control, pricing, and congestion-sensitive demand. SLO-aware serving and autoscaling systems develop serving policies and capacity control mechanisms to meet latency targets under provisioning frictions (e.g., MArk [4] and QLM [5]), and they typically treat demand as exogenous. GPU pricing systems study pricing mechanisms and charging models for GPU resources, emphasizing price formation and price–resource mismatch [13]. In queueing and congestion models, dynamic pricing uses price together with delay information to shape demand [14, 15, 16]. Related leader–follower formulations appear in large-population network settings [17], in congestion pricing with heterogeneous users [18], and in cloud pricing and provisioning models [19, 20]. These queueing and Stackelberg game models provide equilibrium demand responses under congestion. Building on these ideas, we study a SLO-oriented multi-tenant GPU cloud problem with endogenous demand under provisioning frictions and derive a computable drainability guardrail together with an online action shield for safe learning. Contributions.  We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We formulate joint pricing and scaling in multi-tenant GPU cloud platforms with provisioning frictions as a large-population Stackelberg game problem, yielding an endogenous equilibrium demand map that responds to pricing and congestion.

  • •

    For the reduced fixed price-capacity recursion, we identify an undrainability mechanism in the high-congestion regime and derive a computable drainability guardrail to certify negative drift. Under this guardrail we prove the system admits a unique operating point with global convergence under a checkable step-size condition.

  • •

    We translate this drainability guardrail into an optimizer-agnostic action shield for the full dynamic problem and empirically demonstrate that it serves as a practical safety mechanism for model-free RL in this setting, enabling safe exploration and improving robustness under burst demand shifts.

II Model and Problem Formulation

We consider discrete decision epochs t=0,1,…t=0,1,\dots with interval Δ>0\Delta>0. At each epoch, the platform, leader, first observes the current system state sts_{t} and chooses an action at=(Pt,Sttar)a_{t}=(P_{t},S_{t}^{\mathrm{tar}}) consisting of a unit price and a capacity target. Meanwhile, the chosen target capacity requests enter a pending setup pipeline and gradually translate into active service capacity, while scale-down remains inertial. Given the posted price PtP_{t} and a public congestion signal DtD_{t}, tenants, followers, choose stage-wise submission rates, which generate endogenous demand. The resulting aggregate demand enters the queueing recursion, interacts with the currently active capacity, and determines the next-state update.

The state is defined as st:=(Qt,St,Bt,Sttar,prev)∈𝒮s_{t}:=(Q_{t},S_{t},B_{t},S_{t}^{\mathrm{tar,prev}})\in\mathcal{S}, where QtQ_{t} is the backlog, StS_{t} is the active GPU capacity, BtB_{t} is the pending setup pipeline, and Sttar,prevS_{t}^{\mathrm{tar,prev}} records the previous capacity target to capture target-change dynamics. Here, the setup pipeline represents requested capacity that has not yet become active. It decreases through activation and may be partially canceled after target decreases. The feasible state space is 𝒮:=ℝ+×[0,Smax]×[0,Bmax]×[0,Smax].\mathcal{S}:=\mathbb{R}_{+}\times[0,S_{\max}]\times[0,B_{\max}]\times[0,S_{\max}]. The action of the leader is defined as at:=(Pt,Sttar)∈𝒜a_{t}:=(P_{t},S_{t}^{\mathrm{tar}})\in\mathcal{A}, where PtP_{t} is the posted unit price and SttarS_{t}^{\mathrm{tar}} is the capacity target. The feasible action space is 𝒜:=[Pmin,Pmax]×[0,Smax],Pmin>0\mathcal{A}:=[P_{\min},P_{\max}]\times[0,S_{\max}],P_{\min}>0. We model the public congestion signal using the queue-based delay proxy [21]:

D⁡(Qt,St):=QtSt​μ+ϵ,D(Q_{t},S_{t}):=\frac{Q_{t}}{S_{t}\mu+\epsilon}, (1)

where μ>0\mu>0 is the service rate per GPU and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is a small baseline constant. For brevity, we denote the delay proxy D⁡(Qt,St)D(Q_{t},S_{t}) as DtD_{t}.

II-A Large-Population Demand Response

We model a large population of tenants partitioned into KK mean-field types with density ρk≥0\rho_{k}\geq 0 and ∑k=1Kρk=1\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}=1. At each epoch, given the posted price PtP_{t} and the public congestion signal DtD_{t}, we assume each type chooses its submission rate myopically. We further assume that the coupling across types arises only through the shared congestion signal and the resulting queue recursion. Type kk is characterized by

θk:=(wk,SLOk),wk>0,SLOk∈(0,∞],\theta_{k}:=(w_{k},\mathrm{SLO}_{k}),\ \ w_{k}>0,\ \ \mathrm{SLO}_{k}\in(0,\infty], (2)

where smaller SLOk\mathrm{SLO}_{k} implies higher delay sensitivity, and SLOk=∞\mathrm{SLO}_{k}=\infty represents delay-insensitive residual types. We encode delay sensitivity via the SLO-risk coefficient: δk:=α/SLOk,α>0\delta_{k}\ :=\ \alpha/\mathrm{SLO}_{k},\alpha>0, and thus SLOk=∞\mathrm{SLO}_{k}=\infty yields δk=0\delta_{k}=0. Given (Pt,Dt)(P_{t},D_{t}), a representative type-kk tenant selects a submission rate λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 by solving

maxλ≥0wk​log⁡(1+λ)−(Pt+δk​Dt)​λ,\max_{\lambda\geq 0}\ \ w_{k}\log(1+\lambda)-(P_{t}+\delta_{k}D_{t})\lambda, (3)

where wkw_{k} scales the utility of type kk. The concave log⁡(1+λ)\log(1+\lambda) utility captures diminishing returns, and the linear term captures per-unit monetary and delay-related costs [22]. This strictly concave problem admits the unique solution

λk∗​(Pt,Dt)=[wkPt+δk​Dt−1]+,\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(P_{t},D_{t})=\Big[\frac{w_{k}}{P_{t}+\delta_{k}D_{t}}-1\Big]_{+}, (4)

where [x]+:=max⁡{x,0}[x]_{+}:=\max\{x,0\}. Hence λk∗\lambda_{k}^{\ast} is non-increasing in both PtP_{t} and DtD_{t}, and for δk=0\delta_{k}=0 it is independent of congestion. Aggregating across types yields the endogenous equilibrium demand map Λ∗​(st,at):=∑k=1Kρk​λk∗​(Pt,D⁡(Qt,St)).\Lambda^{\ast}(s_{t},a_{t}):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}\,\lambda_{k}^{\ast}\!\big(P_{t},D(Q_{t},S_{t})\big).

II-B Queueing and Frictional Provisioning Dynamics

The backlog follows a discretized fluid recursion with endogenous demand Λ∗​(st,at)\Lambda^{\ast}(s_{t},a_{t}) and service rate St​μS_{t}\mu:

Qt+1=[Qt+Δ⁡(Λ∗​(st,at)−St​μ)]+.Q_{t+1}=\Big[\,Q_{t}+\Delta\big(\Lambda^{\ast}(s_{t},a_{t})-S_{t}\mu\big)\Big]_{+}. (5)

We model, new capacity requests enter a pending pipeline due to cold starts and setup delays, which is getting completed gradually, while scale-down of active capacity is inertial. Let ω,ν∈(0,1]\omega,\nu\in(0,1] and χ∈[0,1]\chi\in[0,1], where ω\omega is the activation rate of the pipeline, ν\nu captures scale-down inertia [23], and χ\chi is the fraction of a target-decrease that can cancel pending pipeline. We decompose target changes into the target-increase component UtU_{t} and the target-decrease component VtV_{t} as, Ut:=[Sttar−Sttar,prev]+,Vt:=[Sttar,prev−Sttar]+.U_{t}:=[S^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t}-S^{\mathrm{tar,prev}}_{t}]_{+},V_{t}:=[S^{\mathrm{tar,prev}}_{t}-S^{\mathrm{tar}}_{t}]_{+}. At:=min⁡{ω​Bt,Smax−St},A_{t}:=\min\{\omega B_{t},\;S_{\max}-S_{t}\}, (6)

and the canceled pending pipeline mass is

Ct:=min⁡{χ​Vt,Bt−At+Ut}.C_{t}:=\min\{\chi V_{t},\;B_{t}-A_{t}+U_{t}\}. (7)

Bt+1\displaystyle B_{t+1} =Proj[0,Bmax](Bt−At+Ut−Ct),\displaystyle=\Proj_{[0,B_{\max}]}\!\big(B_{t}-A_{t}+U_{t}-C_{t}\big), (8)

where Proj[a,b](x):=min⁡{max⁡{x,a},b}\Proj_{[a,b]}(x):=\min\{\max\{x,a\},b\} denotes projection onto [a,b][a,b].

Given the stage-wise demand response and the induced deterministic state transition, the leader seeks a policy π={πt:𝒮→𝒜}t≥0\pi=\{\pi_{t}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}\}_{t\geq 0} to maximize the infinite-horizon discounted return

−Φ0​Ξ​(s,a),\displaystyle\quad-\Phi_{0}\,\Xi(s,a), (11)

III Fixed-pair backlog recursion and residual regime

This section studies the fixed-pair backlog recursion that underlies the guardrail analysis. Whereas Section II considers the leader dynamically chooses a price–target pair (Pt,Sttar)(P_{t},S_{t}^{\mathrm{tar}}) under provisioning frictions, here we analyze a reduced fixed-pair model by assuming constant price and service capacity (P,S)(P,S). This reduction lets us focus on the key question of drainability: whether backlog can be driven down from high-backlog states under admissible price and service capacity once delay-sensitive demand drops out. In this reduced model, SS denotes effective service capacity in the induced backlog recursion rather than the target variable of the complete model.

We first characterize the residual-demand regime, then derive an explicit drainability guardrail, and finally establish operating-point existence, uniqueness, and global convergence under a checkable step-size condition. From the Stackelberg viewpoint, this analysis isolates how a fixed leader price–capacity choice shapes follower-side residual demand, and it will later serve as the local safety certificate behind the online action shield.

In the fixed-pair model the corresponding recursion of (5) is given by:

Qt+1=FP,S​(Qt):=[Qt+Δ⁡(ΛP,S∗​(Qt)−S​μ)]+,Q_{t+1}=F_{P,S}(Q_{t}):=\Big[\,Q_{t}+\Delta\big(\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q_{t})-S\mu\big)\Big]_{+}, (13)

where the stage-wise equilibrium demand is given by

D⁡(Q):=QS​μ+ϵ,λk∗​(Q):=λk∗​(P,D⁡(Q)),\displaystyle D(Q):=\frac{Q}{S\mu+\epsilon},\qquad\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(Q):=\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(P,D(Q)),
ΛP,S∗​(Q):=∑k=1Kρk​λk∗​(Q).\displaystyle\quad\qquad\qquad\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(Q). (14)

Delay-insensitive types with δk=0\delta_{k}=0, equivalently SLOk=∞\mathrm{SLO}_{k}=\infty, create a residual floor that persists under extreme congestion:

Λ0(P):=∑k:δk=0ρk[wkP−1]+.\Lambda_{0}(P):=\sum_{k:\,\delta_{k}=0}\rho_{k}\Big[\frac{w_{k}}{P}-1\Big]_{+}. (15)

For delay-sensitive types (δk>0\delta_{k}>0), we define the drop-out thresholds as:

Qkdrop​(P,S):=[(S​μ+ϵ)​(wk−P)δk]+,\displaystyle Q^{\mathrm{drop}}_{k}(P,S):=\Big[\,(S\mu+\epsilon)\frac{(w_{k}-P)}{\delta_{k}}\Big]_{+}, (16)
Qdrop(P,S):=maxk:δk>0Qkdrop(P,S).\displaystyle Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S):=\max_{k:\,\delta_{k}>0}Q^{\mathrm{drop}}_{k}(P,S). (17)

Then, the following result formalizes the finite-threshold residual regime.

Proposition 1.

For any fixed (P,S)(P,S) and all Q≥Qdrop​(P,S)Q\geq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S), every delay-sensitive type becomes inactive and ΛP,S∗​(Q)=Λ0​(P).\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q)=\Lambda_{0}(P).

Proof.

If Q≥Qkdrop​(P,S)Q\geq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}_{k}(P,S) and δk>0\delta_{k}>0, then P+δk​D​(Q)≥wkP+\delta_{k}D(Q)\geq w_{k}, hence λk∗​(Q)=0\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(Q)=0 by (4); taking the maximum over δk>0\delta_{k}>0 yields the result. ∎

III-A Guardrail and Structural Drainability

Under fixed (P,S)(P,S), structural drainability means uniformly negative high-backlog drift. By Proposition 1, this is equivalent to requiring service capacity to dominate the residual floor. Then, we define the drainability guardrail formally as follows.

Definition 1 (Drainability guardrail).

A fixed pair (P,S)(P,S) satisfies the drainability guardrail if

Λ0​(P)<S​μ.\Lambda_{0}(P)<S\mu. (18)

Moreover, define residual slack as: ε⁡(P,S):=S​μ−Λ0​(P).\varepsilon(P,S):=S\mu-\Lambda_{0}(P).

The next proposition shows that the guardrail yields uniform negative drift once the system enters the residual regime.

Proposition 2.

If (18) holds, then for all Q≥Qdrop​(P,S)Q\geq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S), ΛP,S∗​(Q)−S​μ=−ε⁡(P,S)<0.\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q)-S\mu=-\,\varepsilon(P,S)<0.

Proof.

Immediate from Proposition 1 and (18). ∎

The next statement characterizes structural non-drainability when the guardrail is violated.

Proposition 3.

If Λ0​(P)>S​μ\Lambda_{0}(P)>S\mu, then for any Q0≥0Q_{0}\geq 0, Qt≥Q0+t​Δ​(Λ0​(P)−S​μ),∀t≥0,Q_{t}\geq Q_{0}+t\Delta\big(\Lambda_{0}(P)-S\mu\big),\forall t\geq 0, so the backlog diverges, and no operating point exists. On the other hand, if Λ0​(P)=S​μ\Lambda_{0}(P)=S\mu, then the residual-regime drift is zero and Qt+1=QtQ_{t+1}=Q_{t} for all tt once Qt≥Qdrop​(P,S)Q_{t}\geq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S).

Proof.

If Λ0​(P)>S​μ\Lambda_{0}(P)>S\mu, then ΛP,S∗​(Q)≥Λ0​(P)>S​μ\Lambda_{P,S}^{\ast}(Q)\geq\Lambda_{0}(P)>S\mu for all Q≥0Q\geq 0, so FP,S​(Q)>QF_{P,S}(Q)>Q on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}. Hence no feasible operating point exists. If Λ0​(P)=S​μ\Lambda_{0}(P)=S\mu, then for any Qt≥Qdrop​(P,S)Q_{t}\geq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S), Proposition 1 gives ΛP,S∗​(Qt)=Λ0​(P)\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q_{t})=\Lambda_{0}(P). Substituting this into (13) yields Qt+1=QtQ_{t+1}=Q_{t}, so the drift is zero. ∎

III-B Operating Point and Global Convergence

We formally define an operating point as a fixed point of the recursion FP,SF_{P,S}, that is, any Q∗≥0Q^{\ast}\geq 0 satisfying

Q∗=FP,S​(Q∗).Q^{\ast}=F_{P,S}(Q^{\ast}). (19)

Equivalently, either Q∗>0Q^{\ast}>0 and ΛP,S∗​(Q∗)=S​μ\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q^{\ast})=S\mu, or Q∗=0Q^{\ast}=0 and ΛP,S∗​(0)≤S​μ\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(0)\leq S\mu. Then, we first establish strict decrease of the demand map above the residual floor.

Lemma 1.

Assume D⁡(⋅)D(\cdot) is strictly increasing. Fix (P,S)(P,S) and define 𝒰⁡(P,S):={Q≥0:ΛP,S∗​(Q)>Λ0​(P)}.\mathcal{U}(P,S):=\{Q\geq 0:\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q)>\Lambda_{0}(P)\}. Then Q↦ΛP,S∗​(Q)Q\mapsto\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q) is strictly decreasing on 𝒰⁡(P,S)\mathcal{U}(P,S). Consequently, for any constant c>Λ0​(P)c>\Lambda_{0}(P), the equation ΛP,S∗​(Q)=c\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q)=c has at most one solution.

Proof.

Take Q2>Q1Q_{2}>Q_{1} with Q1,Q2∈𝒰⁡(P,S)Q_{1},Q_{2}\in\mathcal{U}(P,S). Then at least one delay-sensitive type (δk>0\delta_{k}>0) is active at Q1Q_{1}; otherwise ΛP,S∗​(Q1)=Λ0​(P)\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q_{1})=\Lambda_{0}(P). For such a type, strict monotonicity of D⁡(⋅)D(\cdot) gives P+δk​D​(Q2)>P+δk​D​(Q1)P+\delta_{k}D(Q_{2})>P+\delta_{k}D(Q_{1}), hence λk∗​(Q2)<λk∗​(Q1)\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(Q_{2})<\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(Q_{1}). All other type contributions are non-increasing, so ΛP,S∗​(Q2)<ΛP,S∗​(Q1)\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q_{2})<\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q_{1}). ∎

Following Lemma 1, we provide the result regarding the existence and uniqueness of the operating point as follows.

Proposition 4 (Existence and uniqueness).

Assume D⁡(⋅)D(\cdot) is continuous and strictly increasing with D⁡(0)=0D(0)=0 and limQ→∞D⁡(Q)=∞\lim_{Q\to\infty}D(Q)=\infty. If the guardrail condition (18) holds, then an operating point Q∗Q^{\ast} exists and is unique. Moreover, Q∗=0Q^{\ast}=0 if and only if ΛP,S∗​(0)≤S​μ\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(0)\leq S\mu; otherwise Q∗>0Q^{\ast}>0 and satisfies ΛP,S∗​(Q∗)=S​μ\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q^{\ast})=S\mu.

If f⁡(0)≤0f(0)\leq 0, then Q∗=0Q^{\ast}=0 is an operating point, and it is unique. Indeed, if f⁡(0)<0f(0)<0, monotonicity gives f⁡(Q)<0f(Q)<0 for all Q>0Q>0, so no positive root exists; if f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, any other root Q~>0\widetilde{Q}>0 would satisfy ΛP,S∗​(Q~)=S​μ>Λ0​(P)\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(\widetilde{Q})=S\mu>\Lambda_{0}(P), hence Q~∈𝒰⁡(P,S)\widetilde{Q}\in\mathcal{U}(P,S), which is impossible by Lemma 1.

Now, to control transients, we next show that trajectories enter a bounded absorbing set in finite time.

Lemma 2.

Assume (18) and define Λmax​(P):=∑k=1Kρk​[wkP−1]+.\Lambda_{\max}(P):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}\Big[\frac{w_{k}}{P}-1\Big]_{+}. Moreover, every trajectory enters 𝒬⁡(P,S)\mathcal{Q}(P,S) in finite time.

Proof.

By Proposition 2, for Qt≥Qdrop​(P,S)Q_{t}\geq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S) we have ΛP,S∗​(Q)−S​μ=−ε⁡(P,S)<0\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q)-S\mu=-\varepsilon(P,S)<0, so Qt+1≤[Qt−Δ​ε​(P,S)]+Q_{t+1}\leq[Q_{t}-\Delta\varepsilon(P,S)]_{+}. Hence large backlogs decrease and reach [0,Qdrop​(P,S)][0,Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S)] in finite time. Also, for Qt≤Qdrop​(P,S)Q_{t}\leq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S), P+δk​D​(Q)≥PP+\delta_{k}D(Q)\geq P implies λk∗​(Q)≤[wkP−1]+\lambda_{k}^{\ast}(Q)\leq[\frac{w_{k}}{P}-1]_{+}, so ΛP,S∗​(Q)≤Λmax​(P)\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S}(Q)\leq\Lambda_{\max}(P). Therefore, Qt+1≤Qdrop​(P,S)+Δ​Λmax​(P)Q_{t+1}\leq Q^{\mathrm{drop}}(P,S)+\Delta\Lambda_{\max}(P), proving forward invariance and finite-time entry. ∎

We then impose a checkable step-size condition to guarantee order preservation of the induced map.

Assumption 1.

There exists LΛ​(P,S)L_{\Lambda}(P,S) such that ΛP,S∗\Lambda^{\ast}_{P,S} is LΛ​(P,S)L_{\Lambda}(P,S)-Lipschitz on the forward-invariant region, and

Δ​LΛ​(P,S)≤1.\Delta\,L_{\Lambda}(P,S)\leq 1. (20)

Assumption 1 is checkable in practice: Lemma 3 provides the explicit sufficient bound (21), which guarantees (20).

Lemma 3.

Under Assumption 1, the map FP,SF_{P,S} induced by (13) is non-decreasing on the forward-invariant region. Moreover, the following bound is sufficient for (20):

LΛ(P,S)≤1S​μ+ϵ⋅1P2∑k:δk>0ρkwkδk.L_{\Lambda}(P,S)\;\leq\;\frac{1}{S\mu+\epsilon}\cdot\frac{1}{P^{2}}\sum_{k:\,\delta_{k}>0}\rho_{k}w_{k}\delta_{k}. (21)
Proof.

Write FP,S​(Q)=[G⁡(Q)]+F_{P,S}(Q)=[G(Q)]_{+} with G⁡(Q):=Q+Δ⁡(ΛP,S∗​(Q)−S​μ)G(Q):=Q+\Delta(\Lambda_{P,S}^{\ast}(Q)-S\mu). Since x↦[x]+x\mapsto[x]_{+} is non-decreasing, it suffices to show that GG is non-decreasing. For any Q2≥Q1Q_{2}\geq Q_{1} in the forward-invariant region, Assumption 1 gives ΛP,S∗​(Q2)−ΛP,S∗​(Q1)≥−LΛ​(P,S)​(Q2−Q1)\Lambda_{P,S}^{\ast}(Q_{2})-\Lambda_{P,S}^{\ast}(Q_{1})\geq-L_{\Lambda}(P,S)(Q_{2}-Q_{1}), hence G⁡(Q2)−G⁡(Q1)≥(1−Δ​LΛ​(P,S))​(Q2−Q1)≥0G(Q_{2})-G(Q_{1})\geq(1-\Delta L_{\Lambda}(P,S))(Q_{2}-Q_{1})\geq 0 by (20). Therefore FP,SF_{P,S} is non-decreasing.

By (4), only types with δk>0\delta_{k}>0 contribute to the QQ-dependence of ΛP,S∗\Lambda_{P,S}^{\ast}. For δk>0\delta_{k}>0, combining (1) with (4) gives a QQ-slope bounded in magnitude by 1S​μ+ϵ⋅wk​δkP2\frac{1}{S\mu+\epsilon}\cdot\frac{w_{k}\delta_{k}}{P^{2}}, using P+δk​D​(Q)≥PP+\delta_{k}D(Q)\geq P. Then, in the following theorem combining Proposition 4, Lemma 2, and Lemma 3 yields global convergence.

Theorem 1 (Global convergence to the operating point).

Under the conditions of Proposition 4 and Assumption 1, the trajectory of (13) satisfies Qt→Q∗Q_{t}\to Q^{\ast} for any initial Q0≥0Q_{0}\geq 0.

Proof.

By Lemma 2, there exists T<∞T<\infty such that Qt∈𝒬⁡(P,S)Q_{t}\in\mathcal{Q}(P,S) for all t≥Tt\geq T, where 𝒬⁡(P,S)\mathcal{Q}(P,S) is bounded and forward invariant. Under the stage-wise response in Section II, the map FP,SF_{P,S} is continuous, and by Lemma 3, it is non-decreasing on 𝒬⁡(P,S)\mathcal{Q}(P,S).

If QT+1≥QTQ_{T+1}\geq Q_{T}, then QT+2=FP,S​(QT+1)≥FP,S​(QT)=QT+1.Q_{T+2}=F_{P,S}(Q_{T+1})\geq F_{P,S}(Q_{T})=Q_{T+1}. If QT+1<QTQ_{T+1}<Q_{T}, then similarly QT+2=FP,S​(QT+1)≤FP,S​(QT)=QT+1.Q_{T+2}=F_{P,S}(Q_{T+1})\leq F_{P,S}(Q_{T})=Q_{T+1}. Hence, in either case, by induction the tail sequence {Qt}t≥T\{Q_{t}\}_{t\geq T} is monotone. Since 𝒬⁡(P,S)\mathcal{Q}(P,S) is bounded and forward invariant, {Qt}t≥T\{Q_{t}\}_{t\geq T} is bounded in 𝒬⁡(P,S)\mathcal{Q}(P,S), and therefore converges to some Q¯∈𝒬⁡(P,S)\bar{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}(P,S). Continuity of FP,SF_{P,S} gives Q¯=FP,S​(Q¯)\bar{Q}=F_{P,S}(\bar{Q}), so Q¯\bar{Q} is an operating point.

By Proposition 4, the operating point is unique, and therefore Q¯=Q∗\bar{Q}=Q^{\ast} in either case. Thus Qt→Q∗Q_{t}\to Q^{\ast} for any initial Q0≥0Q_{0}\geq 0. ∎

IV Guardrail-Aware Action Shield for Dynamic Control

Theorem 1 provides a stability certificate for fixed price–capacity pairs (P,S)(P,S). In the full problem, however, the leader chooses a sequence of price–target actions at=(Pt,Sttar)a_{t}=(P_{t},S_{t}^{\mathrm{tar}}) under provisioning frictions and discounted rewards, so the fixed-pair analysis in Section III does not by itself yield an end-to-end stability result for the closed-loop control problem we have posed in the beginning. We therefore use the fixed-pair drainability guardrail as a design principle for dynamic control. This section develops the required ingredients for online certification, builds the corresponding action shield, and incorporates it into a filtered control formulation. The resulting guarded formulation serves as the basis for the numerical study in Section V.

IV-A Safe-Price Map and Effective-Capacity Proxy

To improve the robustness of the online shield, we enforce a safety margin ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1): Λ0​(P)≤(1−ζ)​S​μ.\Lambda_{0}(P)\ \leq\ (1-\zeta)\,S\mu. For S∈[0,Smax]S\in[0,S_{\max}], we define the safe-price map as

Psafe​(S):=inf{P∈[Pmin,Pmax]:Λ0​(P)≤(1−ζ)​S​μ},P_{\mathrm{safe}}(S)\!:=\!\inf\Big\{P\!\in\![P_{\min},P_{\max}]:\Lambda_{0}(P)\!\leq\!(1-\zeta)S\mu\Big\},

with Psafe​(S)=+∞P_{\mathrm{safe}}(S)=+\infty if the set is empty. Since Λ0​(P)\Lambda_{0}(P) is non-increasing in PP, Psafe​(S)P_{\mathrm{safe}}(S) is non-increasing in SS. Moreover, Psafe​(S)P_{\mathrm{safe}}(S) is piecewise explicit and can be computed exactly by scanning the finitely many active-set intervals induced by the residual-type breakpoints.

To evaluate whether a proposed target can support the margin guardrail under provisioning frictions, we construct a one-step effective-capacity proxy directly from the dynamics in (6)–(9). Given a state s=(Q,S,B,Star,prev)s=(Q,S,B,S^{\mathrm{tar,prev}}) and a candidate target StarS^{\mathrm{tar}}, define

A⁡(s)\displaystyle A(s) :=min⁡{ω​B,Smax−S},\displaystyle:=\min\{\omega B,\;S_{\max}-S\}, (22)
Seff​(s,Star)\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,S^{\mathrm{tar}}) :=Proj[0,Smax](S+A⁡(s)−ν​[S−Star]+).\displaystyle:=\Proj_{[0,S_{\max}]}\!\Big(S+A(s)-\nu[S-S^{\mathrm{tar}}]_{+}\Big). (23)

Here A⁡(s)A(s) is the one-step activation term inherited from (6), while Seff​(s,Star)S_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,S^{\mathrm{tar}}) is the resulting one-step active capacity induced by the activation and scale-down terms in (9). Thus, Seff​(s,Star)S_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,S^{\mathrm{tar}}) serves as a friction-aware proxy for the service capacity available in the next step under the proposed target.

IV-B Guardrail-Aware Action Shield

We now define an optimizer-agnostic online action shield that filters each proposed action before execution [12]. The shield follows a minimal-intervention principle: when the proposed target can be certified safe, it leaves the target unchanged and adjusts only the price, raising it just enough to satisfy the guardrail. When such certification is infeasible, the shield instead defaults to an emergency action as a best-effort recovery move. For a candidate action a=(P,Star)∈𝒜a=(P,S^{\mathrm{tar}})\in\mathcal{A}, write SeffS_{\mathrm{eff}} as shorthand for Seff​(s,Star)S_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,S^{\mathrm{tar}}). The resulting action shield is defined by

Γ(s,a):={(max⁡{P,Psafe​(Seff)},Star),if ​Psafe​(Seff)<+∞,aemg:=(Pmax,Smax),otherwise.\Gamma(s,a)\!:=\!\begin{cases}\!\big(\!\max\{P,P_{\mathrm{safe}}(S_{\mathrm{eff}})\},S^{\mathrm{tar}}\big),\!\!\!&\!\!\text{if }P_{\mathrm{safe}}(S_{\mathrm{eff}})\!\!<\!\!+\infty,\\[2.84526pt] a_{\mathrm{emg}}\!:=\!(P_{\max},S_{\max}),&\!\!\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (24)

Since the shield acts only at execution time, it can be placed on top of a wide range of planning or learning methods without changing their internal logic. Section V empirically evaluates this guardrail-aware action shield under off-grid execution and in both steady and bursty demand regimes.

IV-C Filtered Control Problem and Truncation Bound

Let the executed actions be a~t=Γ⁡(st,at)\tilde{a}_{t}=\Gamma(s_{t},a_{t}) for proposed at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}, and let dynamics be st+1=f⁡(st,a~t)s_{t+1}=f(s_{t},\tilde{a}_{t}). The filtered Bellman equation is

V∗​(s)=maxa∈𝒜⁡{r⁡(s,Γ⁡(s,a))+γ​V∗​(f⁡(s,Γ⁡(s,a)))},∀s∈𝒮.V^{\ast}(s)\!=\!\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Big\{r\big(s,\Gamma(s,a)\big)+\gamma V^{\ast}\big(f(s,\Gamma(s,a))\big)\Big\},\ \forall s\in\mathcal{S}.

On the bounded discretized planning domain used for computation, the filtered Bellman operator is a contraction, and therefore admits a unique optimal value function [24]. In Section V, we compute the planning benchmark by applying grid-based value iteration (VI) on this guarded discretization. For finite-horizon planning, let Vt(H)V_{t}^{(H)} denote the value function of backward dynamic programming with horizon HH (DP-HH) at stage tt, with terminal condition VH(H)≡0V_{H}^{(H)}\equiv 0. The standard geometric truncation bound then yields

|V∗​(s)−V0(H)​(s)|≤γH1−γ​Rmax,\displaystyle\big|V^{\ast}(s)-V_{0}^{(H)}(s)\big|\leq\frac{\gamma^{H}}{1-\gamma}\,R_{\max}, (25)
Rmax:=sup(s,a)∈𝒮grid×𝒜grid|r⁡(s,Γ⁡(s,a))|<∞.\displaystyle R_{\max}:=\!\!\sup_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{grid}}\times\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{grid}}}\!\!\big|r(s,\Gamma(s,a))\big|<\infty.

V Experiments

Having constructed the guarded control interface in Section IV, we now evaluate its numerical behavior. The conducted experiments address two questions. First, in Section V-B, we test whether the guarded planning interface provides a reliable approximation to the VI benchmark both on the guarded discretization used for planning and under off-grid execution on the continuous dynamics. Second, in Section V-C, we evaluate whether the proposed guardrail-aware action shield improves safety and learning stability in model-free RL for the pricing-scaling task under both steady and bursty demand.

V-A Baseline Setup and Evaluation Protocol

Baseline setup. All experiments share the same baseline instance and default guarded discretization. Table I summarizes system parameters, and Table II specifies the heterogeneous tenant mix, including delay-sensitive types and delay-insensitive types. We use the mixed-resolution backlog grid Q={0,0.5,1,…,5,6,7,…,50}Q=\{0,0.5,1,\dots,5,6,7,\dots,50\}, uniform grids for state variables StS_{t}, BtB_{t}, and Sttar,prevS^{\mathrm{tar,prev}}_{t} with step size 0.50.5, and uniform action grids for StarS^{\mathrm{tar}} (step 0.50.5) and PP (step 0.20.2).

For each grid pair (s,a)(s,a), we first form the executed action a~=Γ⁡(s,a)\tilde{a}=\Gamma(s,a), evaluate the one-step dynamics and reward, and project the resulting next state to the nearest grid point. This yields a deterministic guarded transition table and reward table.

Evaluation protocol. For planning comparisons, we compute an infinite-horizon benchmark (V∞,π∞)(V^{\infty},\pi^{\infty}) by VI and compare it with finite-horizon backward DP-HH on the same guarded transition and reward tables. For off-grid evaluation, these on-grid policies are executed on the continuous dynamics via nearest-neighbor lookup without per-step state projection [25]. We use the following metrics.

On-grid approximation quality is measured by the relative value gap at an initial state s0s_{0},

Gaprel​(H,s0):=|V∞​(s0)−V0(H)​(s0)|max⁡{|V∞​(s0)|,ε},ε=10−12.\!\!\!\!\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathrm{rel}}(H;s_{0})\!:=\!\frac{|V^{\infty}(s_{0})-V_{0}^{(H)}(s_{0})|}{\max\{|V^{\infty}(s_{0})|,\varepsilon\}},\;\varepsilon=10^{-12}. (26)

Here V∞​(s0)V^{\infty}(s_{0}) denotes the infinite-horizon benchmark value at the initial state s0s_{0} computed by VI, and V0(H)​(s0)V_{0}^{(H)}(s_{0}) denotes the stage-00 value returned by finite-horizon backward DP with horizon HH at the same initial state.

Off-grid execution quality is measured by the mean relative return gap

Gapreloff​(H):=𝔼⁡[|JVI−JDP⁡(H)|max⁡{|JVI|,ε}],ε=10−12,\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathrm{rel}}^{\mathrm{off}}(H):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{|J^{\mathrm{VI}}-J^{\mathrm{DP}(H)}|}{\max\{|J^{\mathrm{VI}}|,\varepsilon\}}\right],\quad\varepsilon=10^{-12}, (27)

where the expectation is over perturbed initial states. Here JVIJ^{\mathrm{VI}} and JDP⁡(H)J^{\mathrm{DP}(H)} denote the realized discounted returns obtained by executing the VI and the DP-HH policy on the continuous off-grid dynamics from the same initial state.

For model-free RL experiments, we also report the number of unsafe executed steps and the cumulative crash count. An executed step is regarded unsafe if the realized action violates the guardrail condition at that state, and a crash occurs when the trajectory hits the truncation boundary Q=QmaxQ=Q_{\max}.

V-B Planning Interface Validation

We first test whether finite-horizon backward DP provides a reliable approximation to the VI benchmark on the guarded discretization. To isolate backlog effects, we consider three representative initial loads, qlow=0.05​Qmaxq_{\mathrm{low}}=0.05Q_{\max}, qmid=0.5​Qmaxq_{\mathrm{mid}}=0.5Q_{\max}, and qhigh=0.98​Qmaxq_{\mathrm{high}}=0.98Q_{\max}, and set s0ℓ=(Q0ℓ,S0,B0,S0tar,prev)=(qℓ,0,0,0)s_{0}^{\ell}=(Q_{0}^{\ell},S_{0},B_{0},S_{0}^{\mathrm{tar,prev}})=(q_{\ell},0,0,0) for ℓ∈{low,mid,high}\ell\in\{\mathrm{low},\mathrm{mid},\mathrm{high}\}. For each s0ℓs_{0}^{\ell}, we compute the VI benchmark value V∞​(s0ℓ)V^{\infty}(s_{0}^{\ell}) and the finite-horizon value V0(H)​(s0ℓ)V_{0}^{(H)}(s_{0}^{\ell}) on the same guarded table, and report the relative gap Gaprel​(H,s0ℓ)\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathrm{rel}}(H;s_{0}^{\ell}). Fig. 1 shows that Gaprel​(H,s0ℓ)\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathrm{rel}}(H;s_{0}^{\ell}) decreases monotonically with HH and exhibits an approximately geometric decay across all three initial-state backlogs. The dashed reference curve is of the form C​γHC\gamma^{H} anchored at H0=60H_{0}=60, illustrating that the observed convergence rate is consistent with the standard geometric truncation behavior in discounted DP. This supports the use of moderate finite horizons in the guarded planning interface.

We next assess how well on-grid planned policies transfer to the continuous off-grid dynamics, using the VI policy computed on the same guarded discretization as the reference for the resulting off-grid performance gap. For each horizon HH, we synthesize a DP-HH policy on the guarded table and execute it on the continuous system using nearest-neighbor lookup without per-step state projection; the VI policy π∞\pi^{\infty} is evaluated under the same off-grid protocol. We report the mean relative return gap Gapreloff​(H)\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathrm{rel}}^{\mathrm{off}}(H) defined in (27), where the expectation is over nsamp=30n_{\mathrm{samp}}=30 initial states with Q0Q_{0} uniformly perturbed within ±5\pm 5 (clipped to [0,Qmax][0,Q_{\max}]) and all other coordinates fixed. For representative trajectory plots, we use the reference initial state s0=(0,0,0,0)s_{0}=(0,0,0,0) over the first 120120 steps. Fig. 2 shows that Gapreloff​(H)\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathrm{rel}}^{\mathrm{off}}(H) is larger only at very short horizons and decays quickly, remaining small for moderate HH, indicating that truncation bias dominates the short-HH regime. Consistently, for a representative long horizon H=150H=150, DP-HH and VI yield nearly identical off-grid backlog trajectories over the first 120120 steps.

V-C Guardrail Effects in Model-Free RL

We next test whether the proposed action shield improves execution safety and training stability in model-free RL. We compare unshielded and shielded tabular Q-learning to isolate the action shield as an execution-time safety layer. Both agents are trained on the same discretized table and executed on the continuous off-grid dynamics via nearest-grid state lookup. Training uses 80008000 episodes of length 200200, with step size α=0.15\alpha=0.15 and an ϵ\epsilon-greedy schedule decaying from 1.01.0 to 0.050.05 over the first 80%80\% of training.

Every 400400 episodes, we run greedy evaluation rollouts of length 250250 and record the mean number of unsafe executed steps; we also track the cumulative number of training episodes that crash by hitting the truncation boundary. As shown in Fig. 3, guardrail-aware action shield drives unsafe executions to zero and substantially suppresses crash accumulation, indicating that it blocks unsafe exploratory actions that would trigger rapid backlog growth. Without the action shield, exploration repeatedly enters a residual-demand regime, leading to frequent crashes. Overall, the results corroborate the drainability analysis and highlight the action shield as an effective mechanism for safe exploration.

Finally, we test whether the shielded policy can preserve safe and stable operation under a burst demand shift. To this end, we stress-test the learned policy under an out-of-distribution demand perturbation relative to the steady-demand training setting [26]. Concretely, we scale the utility weights of all tenant types by a factor of 33 during the time window t∈[40,70)t\in[40,70), i.e., wk​(t)=3​wkw_{k}(t)=3w_{k} during the burst and wk​(t)=wkw_{k}(t)=w_{k} otherwise. We use a mild initial condition s0burst=(0,2,2,1)s_{0}^{\mathrm{burst}}=(0,2,2,1) so that both policies remain well-behaved before the burst. We evaluate greedy policies learned under steady demand, with no exploration during evaluation: the unshielded policy executes at=arg⁡maxa​Q^​(st,a)a_{t}=\arg\max_{a}\widehat{Q}(s_{t},a), while the shielded policy executes a~t=Γ⁡(st,at)\tilde{a}_{t}=\Gamma(s_{t},a_{t}) using a time-varying guardrail recomputed under the current wk​(t)w_{k}(t).

Fig. 4 shows a clear separation. The unshielded policy frequently proposes prices below the guardrail threshold, enters an effectively undrainable regime, and drives the backlog toward the truncation boundary. In contrast, shielded execution keeps the realized actions guardrail-feasible throughout, raises the executed price to the elevated safe threshold during the burst, maintains bounded backlog dynamics, and returns to a stable operating level after the burst subsides. Overall, the burst test shows that action shield improves robustness to abrupt demand shifts, whereas the unshielded policy fails to recover safely.

Taken together, these experiments support two empirical claims: finite-horizon planning reliably approximates the VI benchmark on guarded tables and transfers well to off-grid execution, while guardrail-aware action shield substantially improves safety and stability in model-free RL under both steady and bursty demand.

VI Conclusion and future work

In this work, we have studied the joint pricing-and-scaling control problem in multi-tenant GPU cloud platforms with provisioning frictions and heterogeneous demand through a large-population Stackelberg game formulation. The model assumes the demand is endogenous to posted prices and congestion, and reveals a residual-demand mechanism under extreme congestion that can render the backlog structurally undrainable under bounded price and capacity. To address this, we have analyzed a fixed-pair backlog recursion, proved operating-point uniqueness and global convergence under a checkable step-size condition, and derived an interpretable drainability guardrail that certifies uniform negative drift in the residual regime. Building on the insights from the fixed-pair backlog recursion, we have proposed a piecewise-explicit safe-price map and an optimizer-agnostic action shield for the dynamic problem. Furthermore, the experiments have shown that the proposed guardrail-aware control interface provides a reliable planning approximation and improves the safety and robustness of model-free RL for this pricing and scaling task under off-grid execution and demand shifts.

The present analysis has adopted a deterministic stage-wise demand model and a stylized queue-based congestion proxy to keep the closed-loop structure explicit and tractable. An important direction for future work would be to extend the framework to stochastic demand and service dynamics. Nevertheless, our framework suggests a tractable way to combine equilibrium demand modeling, safety certification, and learning-based control in congestion-sensitive systems with endogenous demand and delayed capacity adjustment.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
